That measured run was House-only; the Senate LIS menu route landed 2026-09-21 (9c58095), so both chambers are now acquired and published, bounded by the same per-run cap on how many roll calls are fetched, newest first. A roll call already published with a tally is not fetched again, so a steady-state run is meant to read only new ones plus the newest few, which are re-read in case the publisher corrected them. **The skip is design, not measurement**: D1 was a cold start, so nothing was held and nothing was skipped, and the saving described here has not been observed yet — the second run is what measures it. Each chamber's own session index is its population: the Senate LIS menu, and the House Clerk's EVS index pages (spicy-docs `list_house_votes`); both hosts are keyless, so the rollup uses no api.data.gov key. A set of roll calls reached from bills alone is not an index of a session's roll calls and never establishes a complete selection. The scheduled scope is the sitting Congress; an earlier Congress is backfilled by dispatching its number, read newest first under the same cap, and once held is never re-read, because the overlap re-read applies to a sitting Congress only. The Clerk and LIS files reach the 101st Congress; the bill family's references reach the 108th. A House roll call that a bill's own action names can be published a cron before the Clerk's index lists it, since the references are read independently and the Clerk file is addressable from the roll-call key alone; such a row carries the same tally and member positions as any other, so this widens timeliness rather than the coverage claim. `vote_date` keeps the Clerk's own spelling (`9-Sep-2025`), which does not sort as a date, so no range over it is quoted here.
